item.research_question: How does the high-entropy strategy, specifically doping rare earth elements at the A-site and Ce at the B-site, influence the corrosion resistance of rare earth zirconates against CMAS molten salt compared to single-component zirconates?
item.processing_route: Solid-phase reaction: raw materials (RE2O3, ZrO2, CeO2) ball-milled at 300 rpm for 24 h, dried at 60 °C, calcined at 1400 °C for 6 h, compacted at 10 MPa uniaxial and 200 MPa cold isostatic pressure, sintered in air at 1650 °C for 10 h
item.test_conditions: CMAS glass powder (33 mol.% CaO, 9 mol.% MgO, 13 mol.% AlO1.5, 45 mol.% SiO2) applied at 30 mg/cm2 on ceramic disks (20 mm diameter, 3 mm thickness), corroded at 1300 °C for 2, 4, and 8 h
key_findings: HEC-0.2 consistently displayed the lowest corrosion layer thickness at all corrosion durations (2, 4, and 8 h).
La2Zr2O7 exhibited the largest corrosion layer thickness under all corrosion durations compared to high-entropy samples.

Rare earth elements with larger ionic radii (e.g., Sm) showed higher content in rod-shaped apatite corrosion products, while those with smaller radii (e.g., Er) showed higher content in spherical ZrO2 products.
The HEC-0 sample exhibited a pyrochlore–fluorite dual-phase structure with a smaller grain size (1.10 ± 0.61 μm) compared to single-phase fluorite samples.
No detectable concentrations of Mg and Al were observed in the corrosion reaction layer throughout the 8 h process.
The melting point of the prepared CMAS glass was determined to be 1237 °C, which is lower than the test temperature of 1300 °C.
The high-entropy strategy significantly reduced the RE:Ca and RE:Si ratios in apatite for the x=0.2 sample, indicating hindered diffusion.
item.mechanism: The high-entropy strategy induces a 'hysteretic diffusion effect' due to the different diffusion rates of various rare earth elements, which retards the mutual diffusion between rare earth elements and Ca/Si from the melt. This leads to the formation of a fine-grained, dense apatite layer that effectively hinders CMAS infiltration. Larger ionic radius rare earth elements preferentially dissolve in apatite, while smaller ones stabilize ZrO2, creating a stable barrier layer.
quotes: The high-entropy sample facilitates the formation of a stable apatite phase, thereby enhancing the corrosion layer's stability and effectively retarding the infiltration of CMAS melt.
The suppression of diffusion evidently enhances the corrosion resistance of rare earth zirconates.
Among them, the high-entropy component HEC-0.2 exhibits the highest level of corrosion resistance due to its ability to maximize the hysteretic diffusion effect of high entropy.

Question: How does the high-entropy strategy, specifically doping rare earth elements at the A-site and Ce at the B-site, influence the corrosion resistance of rare earth zirconates against CMAS molten salt compared to single-component zirconates?. System: (La0.2Sm0.2Dy0.2Er0.2Gd0.2)2(Zr1−xCex)2O7 (x = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5) and La2Zr2O7. Processing: Solid-phase reaction: raw materials (RE2O3, ZrO2, CeO2) ball-milled at 300 rpm for 24 h, dried at 60 °C, calcined at 1400 °C for 6 h, compacted at 10 MPa uniaxial and 200 MPa cold isostatic pressure, sintered in air at 1650 °C for 10 h. Test conditions: CMAS glass powder (33 mol.% CaO, 9 mol.% MgO, 13 mol.% AlO1.5, 45 mol.% SiO2) applied at 30 mg/cm2 on ceramic disks (20 mm diameter, 3 mm thickness), corroded at 1300 °C for 2, 4, and 8 h.
